text: Chapter 2's lab built a working call against the WeatherAPI REST Message, using its getCurrentConditions Function to fetch current conditions for a city. That script works, on the happy path. This lab hardens that exact call with everything Chapter 6 has covered: a try/catch around the call, exponential backoff retrying up to three times on a timeout or server error, a hard rule against ever retrying a client error, and structured logging recording the status code and city on every failure.

Start by isolating the call inside a try/catch. That alone doesn't retry anything yet, but it's the foundation — nothing downstream can throw past this point without the script deciding what happens next. Notice setHttpTimeout, set to ten seconds: it's a real method on the request object that bounds how long execute waits before giving up, which is exactly what turns an indefinite hang into a failure the retry logic can actually react to.

RESTMessageV2's execute generally doesn't throw for an HTTP-level failure — a 4xx or 5xx still comes back as a normal response, just with that status code. A transport failure, where the host was unreachable or no response ever came back, shows up differently: getErrorMessage returns a non-empty string. Checking both together makes the retry decision correct. The one rule that matters most: a 4xx means the request itself is wrong, so retrying an identical request produces an identical failure. Only a 5xx or transport failure justifies a retry.

Now that retryable branch gets wrapped in the same doubling-delay loop from Lesson 21. Trace a real server error through it: attempt one gets HTTP 503, logs a warning with the city and status code, sleeps one second, doubles the backoff to two. Attempt two gets 503 again, logs again, sleeps two seconds, doubles to four. Attempt three finally gets 200, logs the success with which attempt it took, and returns the parsed data — four attempts total, each one logged with enough detail to answer what happened without re-running anything.

Every piece here earns its place. The timeout turns a hang into a failure. The status-code and transport-error check together catch both kinds of failure RESTMessageV2 can produce. The 4xx branch stops a doomed retry before it wastes an attempt. The backoff loop gives a struggling system real recovery room instead of hammering it harder. And the structured logging means whoever looks at this later can tell exactly which city failed, with what status code, on which attempt, without reproducing the failure first.

This is close to exactly what Chapter 8's Capstone asks you to build for its own integration in Lesson 28 — the same three ingredients, applied to a different external system. Next up, Chapter 7 turns to a different integration constraint: what a MID Server does, and why on-premises systems need one standing between them and the ServiceNow cloud instance.
